How to Play Minesweeper

Learn the rules, then start a free game.

Play MinesweeperStrategyControlsNumber Patterns

The goal

Clear every safe square without opening a mine. The numbers show how many mines touch a square, including the eight squares around it.

How the numbers work

  • A 1 means one neighboring square contains a mine.
  • A 2 means two neighboring squares contain mines.
  • A blank square has no neighboring mines and usually opens a larger safe area.

Reveal and flag squares

Click a hidden square to reveal it. When you know where a mine is, flag it so you do not open it by mistake. See the complete Minesweeper controls for mouse, mobile, keyboard, and chord actions.

A flag is a note, not proof. You can remove it later if your logic changes.

Difficulty levels

Start with Beginner to learn the board, move to Intermediate for a larger challenge, and use Expert when you are comfortable reading several clues at once.

Simple first move

The first reveal starts a new board and is protected from an immediate mine. After that, use the numbers to decide which squares are safe and which should be flagged.

Your first game: a 5 × 5 example

This worked example contains three mines. Columns run A–E from left to right; rows run 1–5 from top to bottom. Gray squares are covered, pale squares are open, and flags mark proven mines. These diagrams show one fixed board, not the board you will get in a new random game.

1. Open a square and read the clues

Reveal A1. The blank opening spreads across columns A–C and exposes the numbers in column D. D1 is a 1: exactly one of E1 and E2 is a mine. D2 is a 2: exactly two of E1, E2, and E3 are mines. All their other neighbors are already open.

2. Subtract the smaller clue

D2 includes the same E1 and E2 as D1, plus E3. Its mine count is one higher, so E3 must contain that extra mine. Right-click E3 to flag it. On a phone, switch to Flag mode and tap E3.

3. Use the flag to find safe squares

D3 is a 1 and touches E2, E3, and E4. The proven mine at E3 satisfies it, so E2 and E4 are safe. Left-click those squares, or switch back to Reveal mode before tapping them. Each reveals a 2.

4. Finish the board

With E2 known to be safe, D1 forces E1 to be a mine. With E4 safe, D5 forces E5 to be a mine. You can flag E1 and E5, but flags are optional: revealing all 22 safe squares is what wins the game. The final diagram shows all three proven mine locations.

This example has a deduction-only solution. Random Mini and Easy boards can still require a guess. Never copy a pattern without checking which squares are actually covered.

Try Easy Minesweeper or play a 5 × 5 Mini board. For more deductions, read the logic guide.
